title: ⚡ Circuit Builder Lab
description: Welcome to the Circuit Builder Lab! You are a Grade 6 student entering the school science lab for the first time. Over 14 weeks, you will learn to build circuits from scratch — starting with simple series circuits and working your way up to complex designs. Wire up batteries, LEDs, resistors, and switches while keeping your lab safe and your experiments creative. Can you become the Master Electrician by Science Fair day?
subject: physics
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring electricity and circuits over a 14-week science lab program.
Each week presents a lab challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and creativity.
Watch your dashboard — your Lab Stations (Safety, Wiring, Measurement, Design, Testing) are interconnected.
NPCs like Professor Ohm (teacher), Spark (safety mascot), Emma, and Raj react to your decisions.
Random events like power surges and guest engineers will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Rating high — if it drops too low, you will be put on lab probation!
learning_objectives: Understand the difference between series and parallel circuits
Learn to measure voltage, current, and resistance using lab instruments
Apply Ohm's Law (V = I × R) to predict circuit behavior
Practice safe laboratory procedures when working with electricity
Design creative circuits using LEDs, switches, and resistors
Develop teamwork and collaboration skills in a lab setting
cultural_context: School science laboratory, hands-on STEM learning, collaborative experimentation

rounds.round_title: Week 1: First Day in the Lab
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the science lab! The benches are covered with batteries, wires, bulbs, and mysterious components. Professor Ohm welcomes the class and says: 'Before we touch a single wire, we need to understand what electricity is and how to stay safe.' How do you want to start your journey?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your electricity and circuits education.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Spending time on fundamentals now will make every future experiment easier and safer.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important to understand safety rules before starting hands-on experiments?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students entering a bright science lab for the first time, lab benches with batteries and wires, excited faces, Professor writing on whiteboard, welcoming atmosphere

choices.label: A. Electric current is the flow of tiny charged particles called electrons through a conductor like a copper wire
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Electric current is the flow of electrons (tiny negatively charged particles) through a conductor. Conductors like copper, aluminum, and iron have 'free electrons' that can move easily. This flow of charge is what powers everything from light bulbs to computers!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Electric current is a type of light energy that travels through the air from the power station to your house
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Electric current is NOT light energy traveling through the air. Current is the flow of electrons through a physical conductor (like a wire). You might be thinking of electromagnetic waves (like radio or light), which are different from electric current. Current needs a wire or conductor to flow through!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. Rubber and plastic are good conductors of electricity because they are flexible and easy to bend
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Rubber and plastic are actually INSULATORS — they block the flow of electricity, not allow it. That's exactly why wires are coated in plastic or rubber — to protect you from the electric current flowing through the metal wire inside! Good conductors are metals like copper, aluminum, and silver.

choices.label: D. Electricity only flows when a circuit is open, because electrons need space to move around freely
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 It's the opposite! Electricity flows only in a CLOSED circuit — a complete, unbroken loop. An OPEN circuit has a gap (like a switch turned off), which stops the flow of electrons. Think of it like a circular running track: runners can only keep going if the track has no gaps!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: This week's challenge: build your first series circuit! Professor Ohm explains that in a series circuit, all components are connected in a single loop — like a necklace of beads. Current flows through each component one after another. Emma is eager to start building, while Raj wants to draw the circuit diagram first.
rounds.goal: Build a working series circuit and understand how current flows through it.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Planning your circuit before building saves time and components. A good diagram is half the work done.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What happens to the other bulbs in a series circuit if one bulb burns out? Why?
rounds.image_prompt: Close-up of a simple series circuit on a lab bench with a battery, two light bulbs in series, and connecting wires, student hands building it

choices.label: A. In a series circuit, if one bulb burns out, ALL other bulbs go out because the single path is broken
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A series circuit has only ONE path for current to flow. If any component breaks, the entire circuit is broken — like a chain where one broken link stops the whole chain. This is why Christmas lights wired in series all go out when one bulb fails!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. In a series circuit, if one bulb burns out, only that bulb goes out while the others stay lit
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You're describing how a PARALLEL circuit works, not a series circuit. In a series circuit, there's only one path — so if any part breaks, current stops flowing everywhere. Think of it like a water pipe: if you block one section, water stops flowing through the whole pipe.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. In a series circuit, if one bulb burns out, the other bulbs get brighter because they receive more electricity
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 In a series circuit, removing one bulb doesn't give more electricity to others — it breaks the entire circuit! The current stops flowing completely. You might be thinking of parallel circuits, where removing one path CAN change current in other paths.

choices.label: D. In a series circuit, each component receives a different amount of current depending on its position in the loop
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 This is a common misconception. In a series circuit, the SAME current flows through EVERY component — current doesn't get 'used up' as it goes through. Think of it like water in a pipe: the same amount of water flows past every point. Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: This week Professor Ohm introduces parallel circuits — where components are connected in separate branches, like rungs on a ladder. 'In your house, every light switch works independently. That is parallel wiring!' he explains. Your task is to build a parallel circuit and compare it to last week's series circuit.
rounds.goal: Build a parallel circuit and compare its behavior to a series circuit.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Learning to switch between series and parallel thinking shows mental flexibility — a key skill in engineering and life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do homes use parallel circuits instead of series circuits for their lights and appliances?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab bench showing a parallel circuit with two branches, each containing a bright bulb, battery connected, student comparing brightness to series circuit

choices.label: A. In a parallel circuit, each branch receives the full battery voltage, and if one branch breaks, the others keep working
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In a parallel circuit, each branch connects directly to the battery, so each gets the FULL voltage. And since each branch is an independent path, if one breaks, current still flows through the others. This is exactly why your home is wired in parallel — turning off one light doesn't turn off every light in the house!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. In a parallel circuit, the voltage gets divided equally among all the branches, just like in a series circuit
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Voltage divides in a SERIES circuit, not a parallel one. In a parallel circuit, each branch gets the FULL voltage from the battery. It's like having multiple water pipes connected directly to the same water tank — each pipe gets the full water pressure!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. In a parallel circuit, the same amount of current flows through each branch, regardless of the resistance
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 In a parallel circuit, the current DIVIDES among the branches. More current flows through the branch with LESS resistance (it's the easier path). Think of two roads from home to school — more cars take the wider, easier road. Using Ohm's Law (I = V/R), lower resistance means higher current!

choices.label: D. Adding more branches in parallel increases the total resistance of the circuit, making less current flow
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 It's the opposite! Adding more branches in parallel DECREASES the total resistance because you're creating more paths for current to flow. Think of it like opening more checkout lanes at a grocery store — more lanes means less overall 'resistance' to shoppers getting through. So total current from the battery actually INCREASES!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Professor Ohm brings out the voltmeters. 'Voltage is the push that drives electricity through a circuit — like water pressure in a pipe,' he explains. Today you will learn to use a voltmeter to measure voltage across different components. Raj is excited about precise measurements, but Emma just wants to see big numbers!
rounds.goal: Master the use of a voltmeter and understand what voltage means in a circuit.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Accurate measurement and honest data recording are the foundation of all science. Never fudge your numbers!
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you measured a different voltage than you expected, should you change your data to match? Why or why not?
rounds.image_prompt: Student carefully connecting a digital voltmeter across a battery in a circuit, LCD display showing 9V reading, lab bench with organized components

choices.label: A. Voltage is the electrical 'push' or 'pressure' that drives current through a circuit, measured in volts (V)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Voltage is the 'electrical pressure' or 'push' that drives electrons through a circuit. A battery creates this push by having a chemical reaction that separates positive and negative charges. Higher voltage means a stronger push — that's why a 9V battery pushes more current through the same circuit than a 1.5V battery!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Voltage is the same thing as current — they are just two different words for electricity flowing through a wire
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Voltage and current are two DIFFERENT things! Voltage is the PUSH (like water pressure), while current is the FLOW (like the amount of water actually moving). You can have high voltage but low current (like a static shock) or low voltage but high current. They are related by Ohm's Law: V = I × R.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. A voltmeter must be connected in series (in the same loop) with the component you want to measure
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A voltmeter must be connected in PARALLEL (across) the component, not in series. You place the two probes on either side of the component. If you connect a voltmeter in series, it would block current flow because voltmeters have very HIGH resistance! Remember: Voltmeter = Parallel, Ammeter = Series.

choices.label: D. A 9V battery always pushes exactly 9 amps of current through any circuit, no matter what components are in it
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A 9V battery provides 9 VOLTS (the push), not 9 amps of current! The actual current depends on the resistance of the circuit. Using Ohm's Law (I = V/R), a 9V battery with a 9Ω resistor gives 1A of current, but with a 90Ω resistor it gives only 0.1A. The voltage stays at 9V, but current changes based on resistance!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Professor Ohm writes a famous equation on the board: V = I x R. 'This is Ohm's Law — the most important equation in electricity!' he announces. 'Voltage equals Current times Resistance. Today we explore resistors — the components that control how much current flows.' He hands out a bag of colorful resistors to each team.
rounds.goal: Understand resistance, resistor color codes, and apply Ohm's Law.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Ohm's Law is a powerful tool. Once you master it, you can predict and design any circuit. Learning formulas pays off!
rounds.reflection_prompt: How would you explain Ohm's Law to a friend who has never studied electricity?
rounds.image_prompt: Assorted colorful resistors spread on a lab bench, student using color code chart to identify values, Ohm's Law equation on whiteboard, magnifying glass

choices.label: A. According to Ohm's Law (V = I × R), if a 12V battery is connected to a 4Ω resistor, the current will be 3 amps
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Using Ohm's Law: I = V ÷ R = 12V ÷ 4Ω = 3A. You rearranged V = I × R to solve for current (I). This is the most important equation in electricity! If you know any two of V, I, and R, you can always calculate the third. This is how engineers design every circuit in the world.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Resistance makes current flow faster through a circuit because it gives electrons more energy
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Resistance does the OPPOSITE — it SLOWS DOWN current flow, not speeds it up. A resistor opposes the flow of electrons, like a narrow section in a water pipe that reduces the flow. Higher resistance = less current. That's why V = I × R: for the same voltage, more resistance means less current.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. If you double the resistance in a circuit but keep the voltage the same, the current will also double
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 It's the opposite! If you double the resistance with the same voltage, the current is CUT IN HALF. From Ohm's Law (I = V/R), if R doubles, I halves. For example: 12V ÷ 4Ω = 3A, but 12V ÷ 8Ω = 1.5A. Resistance and current have an INVERSE relationship — when one goes up, the other goes down.

choices.label: D. Ohm's Law only works for batteries and doesn't apply to circuits with light bulbs, LEDs, or motors
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Ohm's Law (V = I × R) works for ALL components in a circuit — resistors, bulbs, LEDs, motors, and more. Every component has some resistance, and Ohm's Law describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance for all of them. It's a universal law of electricity!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: It is project week! Professor Ohm announces: 'Design a circuit using at least 3 LEDs that does something creative and useful.' Emma wants to make a traffic light. Raj wants to build a binary counter. The whole class buzzes with excitement. You have the skills — now it is time to create!
rounds.goal: Design and build a creative LED circuit project.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: True creativity is not random — it combines knowledge, imagination, and the courage to try something new.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How did your knowledge of circuits help you be MORE creative, not less?
rounds.image_prompt: Student presenting a colorful LED circuit project, multiple colored LEDs glowing in a creative pattern on a breadboard, proud expression, classmates watching

choices.label: A. An LED only allows current to flow in one direction and needs a resistor to limit current, or it will burn out
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ LED stands for Light Emitting Diode. The word 'diode' means it only allows current in ONE direction (from the longer leg/anode to the shorter leg/cathode). LEDs have very low resistance, so without a resistor to limit the current, too much current flows and burns them out. Always pair an LED with a resistor!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. LEDs work in both directions — you can connect them either way around and they will always light up
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 LEDs are DIODES — they only work in ONE direction! The longer leg (anode) must connect to the positive (+) side, and the shorter leg (cathode) to the negative (-) side. If you connect them backwards, no current flows and the LED stays dark. This one-way property is what makes diodes so useful in electronics!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. LEDs produce light by heating up a metal filament inside them, just like regular incandescent bulbs
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That describes incandescent bulbs, not LEDs! LEDs produce light when electrons pass through a special semiconductor material and release energy as photons (light particles). There's no hot filament — which is why LEDs are much cooler to touch and use far less energy than incandescent bulbs. LEDs are about 10 times more efficient!

choices.label: D. You can connect an LED directly to a 9V battery without any resistor because LEDs automatically control their own current
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 NEVER connect an LED directly to a 9V battery without a resistor! LEDs have very low resistance, so without a resistor, too much current flows and the LED burns out instantly. You need a resistor (usually 220Ω or 330Ω for a 9V battery) to limit the current to a safe level. Using Ohm's Law, you can calculate the right resistor value.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! During today's lab, someone accidentally creates a short circuit — a wire connects directly across the battery terminals with no resistance! Sparks fly, the wire gets dangerously hot, and the circuit breaker trips, plunging the lab into darkness. Professor Ohm stays calm but serious: 'This is why safety matters. Now, how do we respond?'
rounds.goal: Handle a short circuit emergency safely and learn from the incident.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Emergencies test your character. Staying calm, following procedures, and learning from mistakes are what separate good scientists from reckless ones.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What causes a short circuit, and why is it dangerous? How could this have been prevented?
rounds.image_prompt: Science lab with circuit breaker tripped, dim emergency lighting, concerned students and calm teacher, overheated wire on a lab bench, safety equipment visible

choices.label: A. A short circuit happens when current bypasses the load through a very low-resistance path, causing dangerously high current flow
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A short circuit occurs when current finds a path with almost zero resistance (like a wire accidentally connecting both battery terminals directly). By Ohm's Law (I = V/R), if R is very small, I becomes very large! This massive current overheats the wires and can cause fires. Fuses and circuit breakers protect us by cutting off current when this happens.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. A short circuit happens when you use wires that are too short to reach between components in your circuit
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A 'short circuit' does NOT mean the wires are too short! The word 'short' means the current takes a SHORT-CUT — it bypasses the components (like bulbs or resistors) and flows through a very low-resistance path instead. This causes dangerously high current. The name comes from the current taking a 'shortcut,' not from wire length!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. Short circuits are actually safe because when resistance is low, the circuit uses less electrical energy
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Short circuits are VERY dangerous, not safe! While low resistance means less energy per electron, the TOTAL current becomes enormous (I = V/R). This massive current generates extreme heat in the wires, which can melt insulation and start fires. That's why every home has fuses or circuit breakers — they're the last line of defense against short circuits.

choices.label: D. A fuse works by absorbing extra electricity and storing it, like a rechargeable battery for emergencies
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A fuse doesn't store electricity! A fuse contains a thin metal wire that MELTS and breaks the circuit when too much current flows through it. Once the fuse 'blows,' the circuit is broken and current stops — protecting the rest of the circuit from damage. Fuses are sacrificial — they destroy themselves to save your circuit!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Now that everyone understands safety better, Professor Ohm introduces switches — the components that control when current flows. 'Every light switch in your house, every button on your phone, every key on a keyboard is a switch,' he says. 'Today you will design circuits where switches control the flow of electricity in clever ways.'
rounds.goal: Build circuits using different types of switches and understand how they control current.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Switches are about control. The ability to turn things on and off at the right time is the essence of all technology.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How many switches do you interact with every day? How would life be different without them?
rounds.image_prompt: Assortment of switches on a lab bench — toggle switch, push button, slide switch — with a student building a multi-switch circuit, wires neatly organized

choices.label: A. A switch controls a circuit by creating or breaking a gap in the path — when open, the gap stops current; when closed, current flows
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A switch is the simplest circuit controller! When CLOSED (on), the switch completes the circuit path so current can flow. When OPEN (off), it creates a physical gap that stops current. Every light switch, power button, and keyboard key works on this basic principle. Two switches in series create an AND gate — both must be closed for current to flow!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. When a switch is 'open,' the circuit is complete and current flows through; 'closed' means the circuit is broken
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You have it backwards! An OPEN switch has a gap (like an open gate that blocks the road) — current CANNOT flow. A CLOSED switch connects the two terminals (like closing a gate to complete the path) — current CAN flow. Think of it as closing a gap: close the switch = close the gap = current flows!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. Two switches connected in parallel both need to be turned ON for the bulb to light up
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Two switches in PARALLEL create an OR gate — EITHER switch being ON will light the bulb. That's because parallel provides multiple paths. If EITHER path is complete, current flows. You're describing switches in SERIES (an AND gate), where BOTH must be ON because there's only one path. Parallel = OR, Series = AND!

choices.label: D. Switches slow down the current when they are turned on, acting like partial resistors in the circuit
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Switches are NOT resistors — they're binary (on/off) devices. When closed, a switch has almost ZERO resistance, so it doesn't slow current at all. When open, it has INFINITE resistance (a physical gap). Unlike a resistor that partially limits current, a switch is all-or-nothing: it either lets ALL the current through or NONE.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: The challenge level jumps up this week! Professor Ohm draws a complex circuit on the board with BOTH series and parallel sections combined. 'Real-world circuits are never just one type,' he says. 'Your phone, your TV, your car — they all mix series and parallel connections.' Emma looks nervous, but Raj is already sketching in his notebook.
rounds.goal: Design and analyze a circuit that combines series and parallel elements.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Real problems are messy combinations of simple concepts. The ability to break a complex circuit into simpler parts is a superpower.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do you approach a complex problem? Do you try to understand the whole thing at once, or break it into smaller pieces?
rounds.image_prompt: Complex circuit on a breadboard combining series and parallel sections, student analyzing it with a pencil tracing current paths, circuit diagram on paper beside it

choices.label: A. In a combined circuit, you analyze the parallel section first to find its equivalent resistance, then add it to the series resistances
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To solve a combined (series-parallel) circuit, first simplify the parallel section into one equivalent resistance using 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Then treat that equivalent resistance as a single component in series with the other resistors. Add them up to get total resistance. Finally, use Ohm's Law to find current and voltage! Breaking complex problems into simple steps is key.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. In a combined circuit, all components always receive the same voltage and the same current regardless of how they are connected
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 In combined circuits, voltage and current distribute differently depending on the connection. Series components share voltage but have the SAME current. Parallel components have the SAME voltage but share current. In a combined circuit, you need to identify which parts are series and which are parallel to figure out voltage and current for each component.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. You can always just add all the resistor values together to find total resistance, whether they are in series or parallel
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Simply adding resistor values only works for SERIES connections (Rtotal = R1 + R2). For PARALLEL connections, you use 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2, which always gives a SMALLER total than the smallest individual resistor. For example, two 100Ω resistors in parallel = 50Ω, not 200Ω. The method depends on how components are connected!

choices.label: D. Real-world devices like phones and TVs only use series circuits because they are simpler and cheaper to build
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Real-world devices almost ALWAYS use COMBINED circuits — mixtures of series and parallel connections. Your phone has thousands of components in complex arrangements. Pure series circuits have a fatal flaw: if one component fails, EVERYTHING stops. That's why practical devices use parallel branches for reliability and series elements for control.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Professor Ohm introduces a new formula: P = V x I (Power equals Voltage times Current). 'Power tells us how much energy a circuit uses per second,' he explains. 'This is why your electricity bill goes up when you leave lights on!' He challenges the class to calculate the power consumption of their circuits and think about energy efficiency.
rounds.goal: Understand electrical power, calculate power consumption, and think about energy efficiency.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Understanding energy consumption connects science to real-world responsibility. Every watt matters for the environment.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you could redesign one electrical device in your home to use less power, which would it be and how would you do it?
rounds.image_prompt: Student calculating power formula on paper next to a circuit, P=VxI written on whiteboard, energy meter showing watts, LED vs incandescent bulb comparison

choices.label: A. Electrical power is calculated using P = V × I, so a device using 2A of current at 12V consumes 24 watts of power
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Power (P) = Voltage (V) × Current (I). So 12V × 2A = 24 watts. One watt means one joule of energy is used per second. This formula tells you how quickly a device uses electrical energy. A 24W device uses twice as much energy per second as a 12W device. This is why your electricity bill is based on kilowatt-hours (kWh) — power × time!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Power is measured in volts, and the higher the voltage, the more power a device always uses
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Power is measured in WATTS (W), not volts. Voltage is just one part of power. P = V × I means power depends on BOTH voltage AND current. A device at 100V with 0.01A uses only 1W, while a device at 5V with 10A uses 50W! Higher voltage alone doesn't mean more power — you need to know the current too.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. An LED light and an incandescent bulb that produce the same brightness must be using the same amount of power
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 An LED producing the same brightness as an incandescent bulb uses about 1/10th the power! Incandescent bulbs waste about 90% of their energy as heat, while LEDs convert much more energy directly into light. A 10W LED can be as bright as a 100W incandescent bulb. This is why switching to LEDs saves so much money and energy!

choices.label: D. If you leave a 60-watt light bulb on for 1 hour or 10 hours, it uses the same total amount of electrical energy
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Energy = Power × Time. A 60W bulb on for 1 hour uses 60 watt-hours (Wh) of energy, but the same bulb on for 10 hours uses 600 Wh — ten times more! Power tells you the RATE of energy use (per second), but total energy depends on how LONG the device runs. That's why turning off lights saves energy — less time = less total energy used.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Professor Ohm announces a team competition: 'Each team will design, build, and present a working circuit that solves a real problem. You have the full period to plan, build, and test. The best project earns the Circuit Champions trophy!' Emma and Raj are fired up. This is your chance to combine everything you have learned!
rounds.goal: Collaborate with your team to design and build a practical circuit project.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Great teams leverage everyone's strengths. The best projects come from teams where every member feels valued and heard.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What role did you play in your team, and how did it contribute to the final project?
rounds.image_prompt: Team of Grade 6 students huddled around a lab bench, collaborating on a circuit project, one drawing diagrams, one wiring, one testing, energetic teamwork

choices.label: A. Two 100Ω resistors connected in parallel have a combined resistance of 50Ω, which is LESS than either individual resistor
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Using 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 = 1/100 + 1/100 = 2/100, so Rtotal = 100/2 = 50Ω. In parallel, total resistance is ALWAYS less than the smallest individual resistor. This makes sense because you're adding MORE paths for current, which makes it easier (less resistance) for current to flow overall. Two identical resistors in parallel always give half the resistance!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Two 100Ω resistors connected in parallel have a combined resistance of 200Ω, because you add them together
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 200Ω would be correct if they were in SERIES (where Rtotal = R1 + R2). In PARALLEL, you use 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2, giving 50Ω. Parallel resistance is always LESS than the smallest individual resistor because you're opening more paths for current — like opening more doors in a hallway makes it easier for people to get through!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. In a series circuit with a 9V battery and a 3Ω resistor, the current through the circuit is 27 amps
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You multiplied V × R = 27, but Ohm's Law says I = V ÷ R, not V × R. The correct answer is I = 9V ÷ 3Ω = 3A. Remember: to find current, DIVIDE voltage by resistance. A helpful way to remember: cover the 'I' in the V=IR triangle, and you see V/R. 27 amps from a 9V battery would be extremely dangerous!

choices.label: D. Adding a resistor in series to a circuit increases the total current flowing from the battery
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Adding a resistor in series INCREASES total resistance, which DECREASES the current (I = V/R). More resistance means less current, not more. Think of adding a narrow section to a water pipe — it restricts flow. This is actually useful! Resistors are added in series to LIMIT current, which is why LEDs always need a series resistor.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! When you arrive at the lab, you find that half the equipment has malfunctioned — multimeters give wrong readings, some power supplies are dead, and the component bins are nearly empty. The school budget has no emergency funds. Professor Ohm looks worried: 'We need to figure out how to keep learning with limited resources.' The Science Fair is only two weeks away!
rounds.goal: Keep your learning and projects going despite severe equipment limitations.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: The greatest innovations often come from constraints. When resources are limited, creativity and teamwork become your most powerful tools.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can limitations actually make you MORE creative? Think of an example from your own life.
rounds.image_prompt: Science lab with OUT OF ORDER signs on equipment, nearly empty component bins, worried students and teacher brainstorming solutions on whiteboard, resourceful atmosphere

choices.label: A. To troubleshoot a circuit that isn't working, first check if the circuit is complete (no gaps), then check if the battery has charge, then test each component
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Systematic troubleshooting follows these steps: (1) Check for complete circuit path — any gap breaks the circuit. (2) Check the power source — a dead battery means no voltage. (3) Test individual components — use a multimeter to check each one. This logical, step-by-step approach is used by professional electricians and engineers. It saves time compared to random guessing!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. If a circuit stops working, the best approach is to take everything apart and rebuild it from scratch every time
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Tearing everything apart wastes time and components! A systematic approach — checking connections, testing the battery, and isolating each component — finds the problem much faster. Real engineers use a 'divide and conquer' strategy: test the middle of the circuit first to narrow down which HALF has the problem, then keep splitting. Work smarter, not harder!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. You can test if a wire is broken by connecting it to the highest voltage battery available to see if sparks appear
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 NEVER test wires with high voltage to look for sparks — that's dangerous! The safe way to test a wire is to use a multimeter set to 'continuity' mode. It sends a tiny, safe current and beeps if the wire is intact. You can also measure resistance: a good wire shows nearly 0Ω, while a broken wire shows infinite resistance (OL on the display).

choices.label: D. A multimeter set to measure voltage can also tell you the current in a circuit without changing any connections
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Voltage and current require DIFFERENT connections! A voltmeter connects in PARALLEL (across a component) and measures the 'push.' An ammeter connects in SERIES (breaks the circuit and goes in line) and measures the 'flow.' If you try to measure current with voltage settings, you'll get wrong readings. Always match the multimeter setting to what you're measuring!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: One week before the Science Fair! Professor Ohm gives you full creative freedom: 'Use everything you have learned to design the most innovative circuit you can imagine. Think beyond the textbook. What can electricity do that nobody in this class has tried yet?' The lab is buzzing with final preparations and wild ideas.
rounds.goal: Push your creativity and knowledge to design an original, innovative circuit.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Innovation happens when you combine things in new ways. Every great invention started as a 'What if...?' question.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the most surprising thing you learned about circuits this semester? How could you use that in a new way?
rounds.image_prompt: Student sketching futuristic circuit design in notebook, surrounded by components and prototypes, lightbulb moment, creative energy, messy but brilliant workspace

choices.label: A. A circuit breaker works like a reusable fuse — it automatically disconnects the circuit when current is too high, and can be reset
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A circuit breaker detects excessive current and automatically opens (breaks) the circuit to stop current flow — just like a fuse. But unlike a fuse (which melts and must be replaced), a circuit breaker can be RESET and used again by flipping the switch back. That's why modern homes use circuit breakers instead of fuses — they're safer and more convenient!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Static electricity and current electricity are the same thing — they both involve electrons flowing continuously through wires
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Static electricity and current electricity are different! STATIC electricity is a buildup of charge on a surface (like when you rub a balloon on your hair — charges accumulate but don't flow). CURRENT electricity is a continuous FLOW of charges through a conductor (like in a circuit). Static gives sudden discharges (shocks), while current provides steady, usable power.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. Electrons in a circuit travel at the speed of light from the battery to the bulb, which is why lights turn on instantly
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Individual electrons actually move very SLOWLY — only about 1mm per second (called 'drift velocity')! What travels fast is the electrical SIGNAL (the push). Imagine a tube full of marbles: push one in at one end, and one pops out the other end almost instantly — but each marble barely moved. The 'push' travels near light speed, but the electrons themselves drift slowly.

choices.label: D. Thicker wires have MORE resistance than thinner wires because there is more material blocking the electrons
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 It's the opposite! Thicker wires have LESS resistance because they provide MORE space for electrons to flow through. Think of it like a highway: a 4-lane highway (thick wire) has less 'traffic resistance' than a 1-lane road (thin wire). Longer wires have more resistance, and hotter wires have more resistance — but thicker always means less!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Science Fair day is here! The gym is filled with display boards, projects, and excited visitors — parents, teachers, younger students, and even a local newspaper reporter. Your circuit project is set up and ready. Professor Ohm says: 'This is your moment to shine. Show the world what you have learned.' How will you present your work?
rounds.goal: Present your circuit project at the Science Fair and make the most of the experience.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Public presentation takes courage. Whether you win or not, sharing your work with confidence is itself a huge achievement.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, what would you tell your past self about circuits? How much have you grown?
rounds.image_prompt: School Science Fair in a gymnasium, students presenting circuit projects on display boards, parents and teachers visiting, trophy on display, colorful decorations, proud moments

choices.label: A. The total voltage across components in a series circuit always adds up to equal the battery voltage (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) states that the sum of all voltage drops around a closed loop equals zero — meaning the voltage 'used' by the components adds up to exactly what the battery provides. If a 9V battery powers three resistors, and you measure 3V, 4V, and 2V across them: 3+4+2 = 9V! This law always holds true and is essential for circuit analysis.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. In a circuit with a 9V battery and three resistors, each resistor always gets exactly 3V regardless of its resistance value
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Voltage doesn't divide equally unless ALL resistors are EQUAL! In a series circuit, voltage divides in proportion to resistance. A larger resistor 'uses' more voltage. For example, with a 9V battery, a 2Ω and a 1Ω resistor: the 2Ω gets 6V and the 1Ω gets 3V (proportional to their resistance). The total still adds up to 9V (Kirchhoff's Law)!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Batteries create electrons from chemicals inside them and push brand new electrons into the wire
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Batteries don't CREATE electrons — they PUSH the electrons that are already in the wire! The chemical reaction inside a battery creates a voltage (electrical pressure) that pushes existing free electrons through the circuit. Electrons flow out of the negative terminal, through the circuit, and back into the positive terminal. The battery is like a pump, not a factory!

choices.label: D. Once a circuit is turned on, the electricity is 'used up' by each component, so less and less reaches the end of the circuit
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Electricity is NOT 'used up'! The same amount of current (number of electrons) that enters a component also exits it. What IS used is ENERGY — each component converts electrical energy into other forms (light, heat, sound). The electrons keep circulating. It's like water in a fountain: the water isn't used up, it cycles around — but the pump (battery) provides the energy to keep it moving.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

glossary_terms.definition: A closed loop path through which electrical current can flow, typically including a power source, conductors (wires), and one or more loads (like bulbs or LEDs).
A circuit where all components are connected one after another in a single loop. If one component breaks, the entire circuit stops working.
A circuit where components are connected in separate branches. Each branch gets the full voltage, and if one branch breaks, the others keep working.
The electrical pressure or push that drives current through a circuit, measured in volts. Think of it like water pressure in a pipe.
The flow of electric charge through a circuit, measured in amperes (amps). Think of it like the amount of water flowing through a pipe.
The opposition to current flow in a circuit, measured in ohms. Resistors are components specifically designed to provide a known amount of resistance.
The fundamental equation of electricity: V = I x R (Voltage equals Current times Resistance). It lets you predict how a circuit will behave.
A special component that produces light when current flows through it. LEDs are much more energy-efficient than traditional incandescent bulbs.
A dangerous condition where current flows through a path with almost no resistance, causing excessive current that can overheat wires and start fires.
A safety device containing a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if too much current flows, protecting the rest of the circuit from damage.
A measuring instrument that can measure voltage, current, and resistance. Essential lab equipment for analyzing and troubleshooting circuits.
The rate at which electrical energy is used, measured in watts. Calculated as P = V x I (Power equals Voltage times Current).

endings.title: Master Electrician
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Circuit Builder Lab! Your knowledge of circuits is extraordinary, your safety record is impeccable, and your innovative designs have inspired the entire school. Professor Ohm nominates you for the District Science Award, and the local newspaper features your Science Fair project on the front page. You have proven that curiosity, hard work, and creativity can illuminate the world!

endings.title: Skilled Circuit Builder
endings.message: You have become a skilled circuit builder with solid knowledge and good lab practices! Your Science Fair project demonstrates real competence in designing and analyzing circuits. Professor Ohm is proud of your progress and says you are ready for the advanced electronics elective next year. You may not have won the top prize, but your skills are genuine and your future in science is bright!

endings.title: Lab Regular
endings.message: You completed the Circuit Builder Lab program with mixed results. Some weeks were great and others were tough, but you stuck with it and learned the basics of electricity and circuits. Professor Ohm says there is always next semester to improve, and the foundation you built will serve you well. Keep experimenting — every expert was once a beginner!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Circuit Builder Lab was a tough journey for you. Many of the concepts were confusing, and the hands-on work did not always go as planned. But here is the important thing — you did not give up. Professor Ohm arranges extra tutoring sessions for you and says: 'The students who struggle the most often end up understanding the deepest, because they had to fight for every insight.' Your story is not over!

endings.title: Lab Probation
endings.message: Due to repeated safety violations and low safety awareness, Professor Ohm has placed you on Lab Probation. You can only observe experiments — no hands-on work until you pass the safety certification test. It is a tough consequence, but safety in a science lab is non-negotiable. The good news? Spark the safety mascot has volunteered to tutor you personally. This setback is temporary — learn from it and come back stronger!

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: ⚡ Circuit Builder Lab Basics

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in Newtons (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton.

questions.question: What happens when balanced forces act on a stationary object?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces cancel out, so the object remains stationary.

questions.question: Friction always acts in which direction?
questions.explanation: Friction opposes the direction of motion or attempted motion.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of ⚡ Circuit Builder Lab. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 2: ⚡ Circuit Builder Lab Advanced

questions.question: Friction always acts in which direction?
questions.explanation: Friction opposes the direction of motion or attempted motion.

questions.question: Which of Newton's laws says 'every action has an equal and opposite reaction'?
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the advanced concepts covered in rounds 6-10 of ⚡ Circuit Builder Lab. These build on the fundamentals and test deeper understanding.
